items.prompt: Define the balance of trade in goods.
items.canonical_answer: Goods export value minus goods import value over a stated period.
marking_guidance: Definition: exports less imports 1; qualifier: goods and period 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain how higher goods export receipts affect the goods balance if import value is unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Initial change: export receipts rise (1); subtracting unchanged imports gives a higher balance, reducing a deficit or increasing a surplus for the economy (1).
marking_guidance: Initial change: receipts 1; mechanism/effect for economy: balance improves under unchanged-import condition 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain the goods balance with exports N$90 million and imports N$110 million.
items.canonical_answer: Imports exceed exports by N$20 million (1), so it is a goods deficit, not a complete balance-of-payments conclusion (1).
marking_guidance: Context: values; reasoning: difference 1; result: deficit with account limit 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why a goods-trade deficit is not the whole balance of payments.
items.canonical_answer: Goods trade is one category (1), while the wider accounts include services, income, transfers and financial transactions (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: part versus whole; boundary/test: transaction coverage,1 each.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why investment funds from a foreign owner are not automatically a service export.
items.canonical_answer: They finance an investment rather than pay for a service supplied (1), so financial-flow and current-account trade categories must stay distinct (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: incoming money versus export; boundary/test: investment finance or service purchase,1 each.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define currency appreciation under market determination.
items.canonical_answer: A rise in a currency’s value relative to another under market determination.
marking_guidance: Meaning: relative currency value rises 1; qualifier: market-determined comparison 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain how greater foreign demand for an invented economy’s exports could affect its market-determined currency value, other influences unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Initial change: export buyers may need more local currency (1); increased demand relative to supply can raise its value, subject to the stated conversion and unchanged conditions (1).
marking_guidance: Initial change: export demand 1; mechanism/effect for economy: currency demand can appreciate rate under conditions 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why attractive interest returns alone do not guarantee inward investment or currency appreciation.
items.canonical_answer: Investors also assess risk and expected value changes (1), so the final flow and rate depend on their decisions and other currency demand/supply influences (1).
marking_guidance: Context: interest incentive; reasoning: risk/expectations 1; result: conditional flows/rate 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why A can have absolute advantage in cloth and grain while B has comparative advantage in grain: equal resources yield A30 cloth or 15 grain and B12 cloth or 12 grain.
items.canonical_answer: A has greater output in both goods. But grain costs A2 cloth and B1 cloth, so B sacrifices less cloth per grain. Absolute advantage is higher output on equal inputs; comparative advantage is lower opportunity cost.
marking_guidance: Relationship: distinct tests 1; evidence:30/15 versus 12/12 gives 2 and 1 cloth 1; explanation: B lower sacrifice despite A output advantage 2.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why the producer with the greatest output of each good is not automatically the comparative-advantage producer of both.
items.canonical_answer: Comparative advantage depends on relative sacrifice (1), so another producer can have a lower opportunity cost in one good despite lower absolute output (1).
marking_guidance: Context: two-good comparison; reasoning: cost ratio 1; result: raw output insufficient 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain the error in defining comparative advantage as simply making more output with the same resources.
items.canonical_answer: That is the absolute-advantage test (1); comparative advantage requires lower opportunity cost relative to another producer (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: efficiency versus sacrifice; boundary/test: equal-input output versus relative cost,1 each.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Calculate A’s absolute output advantage in cloth when equal resources produce 30 cloth at A and 12 at B.
items.canonical_answer: Formula: A output minus B output. Working:30−12=18. Answer:18 cloth units for the stated equal resources.
marking_guidance: Formula/working for learning; answer/unit: 18 cloth earns the single result mark.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain the absolute-advantage conclusion when equal resources produce 30 cloth or 15 grain at A,12 cloth or 12 grain at B.
items.canonical_answer: A produces 18 more cloth or 3 more grain on the same resource basis, so has absolute advantage in both. The data are alternative maxima and do not show both produced simultaneously. They do not replace opportunity-cost calculations.
marking_guidance: Relationship: more per equal resources 1; evidence:18/3 output differences 1; explanation: alternative maxima and test boundary 2.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why comparing 100 units from ten labour hours with 150 from thirty hours does not establish advantage merely from the larger output.
items.canonical_answer: Input amounts differ (1), so a common output-per-input or input-per-output basis is needed before an efficiency comparison (1).
marking_guidance: Context: unequal hours; reasoning: resource basis differs 1; result: raw total insufficient 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Calculate A’s opportunity cost of one cloth when the same resources can produce 30 cloth or 15 grain.
items.canonical_answer: Formula: grain forgone/cloth produced. Working:15/30=0.5. Answer:0.5 grain per cloth.
marking_guidance: Formula/working shown; answer unit: 0.5 grain per cloth earns the single result mark.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain which producer has comparative advantage in grain if A gives up 2 cloth per grain and B gives up 1.
items.canonical_answer: B has the lower opportunity cost. It sacrifices 1 rather than 2 cloth for a grain unit, so it gives up less alternative output. This comparison concerns sacrifice, not merely which can make more grain in total.
marking_guidance: Relationship: lower opportunity cost 1; evidence:1 versus 2 cloth 1; explanation: comparative not absolute test 2.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why writing 0.5 without grain per cloth is incomplete in A’s opportunity-cost answer.
items.canonical_answer: The ratio could describe either good as the target (1), so units identify what is forgone per unit produced and prevent inversion (1).
marking_guidance: Context:0.5 result; reasoning: target ambiguity 1; result: unit-labelled sacrifice 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: An invented economy’s goods exports rise N$90 toN$105 million while imports remain N$110 million. Foreign investment also finances a workshop, and services data are absent. Its currency is market-determined in this illustration. (a) Describe three transaction features (6). (b) Examine the goods-balance and possible currency implications (7). (c) Suggest evidence needed before judging the wider external position (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Goods export receipts rise 15 million. Imports are unchanged. Workshop investment is financing rather than a service export. (b) The goods deficit narrows 20 to 5 million. Export-related currency demand could rise where conversion is needed, but other flows and expectations affect the rate. The financing inflow is not itself an improvement in goods exports. (c) Obtain services, income, transfer and relevant financing information on a consistent period, as well as currency demand/supply evidence. Consider sustainability rather than infer the whole position from one account. The judgement recognises the narrower goods deficit but withholds unsupported claims about all external transactions or a definite rate.
marking_guidance: Context: economy. Parts/allocation: (a) three features 2 each=6. (b) balance evidence 2, currency mechanism 3, category limit 2=7. (c) missing data 3, consistency/sustainability 2, conditional judgement 2=7. Mechanism: identify the relevant flow or opportunity-cost comparison; judgement retains stated assumptions.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: (a) Define goods trade balance (2). (b) Define appreciation (2). (c) Explain why investment finance differs from service exports (2). (d) Explain one currency-demand channel from trade (2). (e) Explain absolute advantage (2). (f) Explain comparative advantage (2). (g) Explain why common resource data matter (2). (h) Explain why trade terms matter to gains (2).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Goods exports less imports in a period. (b) Relative currency-value rise under market determination. (c) Financing creates a financial transaction rather than service payment. (d) Buyers may need exporter currency, raising demand under relevant conversion conditions. (e) More output from equal resources or fewer inputs for equal output. (f) Lower opportunity cost. (g) Unequal input can explain a bigger total without efficiency advantage. (h) Exchange must provide better relative alternatives after relevant costs for gains to arise.
marking_guidance: Parts/allocation and precision: eight at 2. (a) difference + goods/period; (b) rise + relative market basis; (c) categories contrasted; (d) conversion + demand; (e) output + input basis; (f) lower + forgone alternative; (g) resource difference + fair comparison; (h) terms + net gains condition.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Two invented producers use equal resources. A can make 30 cloth or 15 grain; B12 cloth or 12 grain. These are alternative maximum outputs. A proposed exchange gives one cloth for 0.75 grain; ignore transport and adjustment costs for the initial illustration. (a) Define comparative advantage (2). (b) Explain the absolute-advantage pattern (4). (c) Explain opportunity costs and the possible trade gain (7). (d) Discuss whether the calculation alone proves practical trade should occur (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Lower opportunity cost of the relevant good. (b) A has absolute advantage in cloth 30 versus 12 and grain 15 versus 12 using equal resources. (c) Cloth costs A0.5 grain, B1 grain, so A has comparative advantage in cloth; grain costs A2 cloth, B1, so B has it in grain. Exchanging one cloth for 0.75 grain lets A receive more than its 0.5 sacrifice and B pay less than its 1 sacrifice for cloth, showing possible mutual gain in the illustration. (d) The ratios and terms support a simple potential gain. Actual costs, quality, resource movement and risks could reduce it and were explicitly excluded initially. Judge practical trade after those are assessed; the accounting opportunity alone is not a guarantee of realised welfare for all participants.
marking_guidance: Context: producers. Parts/allocation: (a) lower 1, opportunity cost 1. (b) two common-resource output comparisons 2 each=4. (c) cost evidence 3, specialisation pattern 2, exchange mechanism 2=7. (d) potential benefit 2, practical limits 2, supported conditional judgement 3=7. Mechanism: identify the relevant flow or opportunity-cost comparison; judgement retains stated assumptions.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Evaluate whether an invented analyst should infer a sustained current-account improvement solely from a currency depreciation when export supply is constrained and imported inputs are important (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: depreciation can make domestic-priced exports cheaper to foreign buyers and discourage some imports if trade demand is sufficiently responsive and supply can respond. Against: constrained export capacity limits quantity gains, while unchanged foreign-priced imports and inputs cost more domestic currency. Contracts and response time can delay adjustment. Judgement: assess trade responsiveness, feasible supply and the net import-cost effect before predicting improvement. The condition for the favourable result is adequate quantity response and usable productive capacity; depreciation alone does not establish it.
marking_guidance: Argument for: conditional competitiveness mechanism up to 4. Argument against: supply/input/time limits up to 4. Judgement: distinct responsiveness and supply condition 1. Total 9. Condition: trade quantities and supply response must support the net result.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum
